after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $N$ given that 

$$
N[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), right-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $N:$

$$
N={{[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $N$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $N$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P:$

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$

EXPLANATION

Notice that the matrix [2112] appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), right-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for N:

N=[2112]⏟P[500−1]⏟D[2112]−1⏟P−1

Therefore, N is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of N are λ1=5 and λ2=−1 and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix P:

v1=[21] and v2=[12]

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors of a Matrix Using the Properties of Diagonalization
content.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $N$ given that 

$$
N[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), right-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $N:$

$$
N={{[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $N$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $N$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P:$

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$

decision.explanation: Since N=PDP^{-1}, N^{18}=PD^{18}P^{-1}. Here (2^{1/9})^{18}=4, so D^{18}=diag(1,4). Using P^{-1}=\frac14\begin{pmatrix}3&-5\\-4&8\end{pmatrix}, multiplication gives N^{18}=\begin{pmatrix}-14&30\\-9&19\end{pmatrix}.

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
We have been given the following diagonalization of $N.$

$$
N={{[\begin{aligned}8 & 5 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[9]{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}8 & 5 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

So, since $N=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${N}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{N}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the inverse of the matrix $P.$ We get

$$
{[\begin{aligned}8 & 5 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}].
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}{N}^{18} & =P{D}^{18}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 5 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[9]{2}\end{aligned}]}^{18}[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4} & -\frac{5}{4} \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 5 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{1}^{18} & 0 \\ 0 & (\sqrt[9]{2})^{18}\end{aligned}](\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}8 & 5 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}8 & 5 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}8 & 20 \\ 4 & 12\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-14 & 30 \\ -9 & 19\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
We have been given the following diagonalization of $N.$

$$
N={{[\begin{aligned}8 & 5 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[9]{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}8 & 5 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

So, since $N=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${N}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{N}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the inverse of the matrix $P.$ We get

$$
{[\begin{aligned}8 & 5 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}].
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}{N}^{18} & =P{D}^{18}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 5 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[9]{2}\end{aligned}]}^{18}[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4} & -\frac{5}{4} \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 5 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{1}^{18} & 0 \\ 0 & (\sqrt[9]{2})^{18}\end{aligned}](\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}8 & 5 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}8 & 5 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}8 & 20 \\ 4 & 12\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-14 & 30 \\ -9 & 19\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
A={{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

So, since $A=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${A}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{A}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the inverse of the matrix $P.$ We get

$$
{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{-2}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]=-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{85} & =P{D}^{85}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{85}{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{1}^{85} & 0 \\ 0 & (-1)^{85}\end{aligned}](-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

So, since $M=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${M}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{M}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the inverse of the matrix $P.$ We get

$$
{[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

$$

$$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $C$ given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]C=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), left-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $C:$ 

$$
C={{{[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $C$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $C$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=6$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P.$ Computing $P,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}P={[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, the corresponding eigenvectors are: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$

content.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $C$ given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]C=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), left-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $C:$ 

$$
C={{{[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $C$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $C$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=6$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P.$ Computing $P,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}P={[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, the corresponding eigenvectors are: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
